proposals.before: Zhou judges relied on three penal canons and five methods of listening, with peasants pounding the left stone for grief and the right for appeals—justice forged like metal—yet the statute book still listed twenty-five hundred capital-linked clauses.
proposals.after: Zhou judges relied on three penal canons and five methods of listening, with peasants pounding the left stone for grief and the right for appeals—justice forged like metal—yet the statute book still listed twenty-five hundred offenses under the five punishments.
proposals.reason: 五刑之屬 means offenses classed under the five punishments, not capital clauses; literal error: "capital-linked" is unsupported by the Chinese.

proposals.before: Chenodi and Aidi inherited a tranquil throne and had ruled only briefly, so they heard few capital cases themselves.
proposals.after: Emperor Cheng and Aidi inherited a tranquil throne and had ruled only briefly, so they heard few capital cases themselves.
proposals.reason: 孝成 is Emperor Cheng of Han; literal error: "Chenodi" is a garbled name.

proposals.before: Wang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
proposals.after: Liang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
proposals.reason: 統 is the memorialist 梁統 Liang Tong named in s0050; literal error: surname given as Wang.

proposals.before: The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Wang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
proposals.after: The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Liang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
proposals.reason: 統 is 梁統 Liang Tong; literal error: surname given as Wang.

proposals.before: Please order the ministries to audit every Jianping-era loophole, weigh each reform's costs and moral effect, keep what still serves civilization and repeal what corrupts it, then engrave a stable code that future reigns never need rewrite—the empire will owe you a debt of gratitude.
proposals.after: Please order the ministries to audit every loophole cut in the Chuyuan and Jianping eras, weigh each reform's costs and moral effect, keep what still serves civilization and repeal what corrupts it, then engrave a stable code that future reigns never need rewrite—the empire will owe you a debt of gratitude.
proposals.reason: 初元、建平 names both reign eras; literal error: the Chuyuan era is omitted.

proposals.before: Men as upright as Yu Quan or brilliant as Sima Qian become permanent pariahs after mutilation.
proposals.after: Even men as loyal as Yu Quan, as trustworthy as Bian He, as wise as Sun Bin, as wronged as Xiangbo, as talented as Sima Qian, or as accomplished as Liu Xiang (Zizheng) become lifelong outcasts once they suffer knife and saw.
proposals.reason: The Chinese lists 卞和, 孫臏, 巷伯 and 子政 as well; literal error: four of the six exemplars are omitted.

proposals.before: Second chances like Taijia's reform or Wei Shang's generalship vanish once the law brands a body ruined.
proposals.after: Then Taijia's reform, Duke Mu's hegemony over Qin, Chen Tang's capture of Zhizhi's capital, and Wei Shang's frontier command could never have happened.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names 穆公 and 陳湯 too; literal error: two exemplars are omitted.

proposals.before: Once Wei stood as a kingdom, Chen Qun inherited his father's portfolio and had to defend corporal punishment anew.
proposals.after: Once Wei stood as a kingdom, Chen Ji's son Chen Qun was then Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk; Emperor Wu of Wei issued an order to restore corporal punishment and had Chen Qun set out his father's argument.
proposals.reason: 陳紀子群時為御史中丞 gives Chen Qun's office, and 使群申其父論 means he restated his father's view; literal error: "inherited his father's portfolio" is unsupported.

proposals.before: Wei jurists continued Han codes rooted in Li Kui's Warring States canon.
proposals.after: At this time the old Qin and Han statutes were still used; their text began with Li Kui, teacher of Marquis Wen of Wei.
proposals.reason: 承用秦漢舊律 and 魏文侯師李悝 identify Li Kui as Marquis Wen's teacher; literal error: "Wei jurists" misreads 魏文侯 and the teacher relation is lost.

proposals.before: Case law ballooned: three hundred decree codices plus Bao Xun's 960-scroll marriage register.
proposals.after: Han-era case decisions were also collected as Ordinance A and following, over three hundred chapters, and Minister over the Masses Lord Bao compiled decisions on marriage and litigation as the Legal Comparisons Catalogue, 906 scrolls in all.
proposals.reason: 鮑公 is Lord Bao, Minister over the Masses, and 九百六卷 is 906 scrolls; literal error: "Bao Xun" and "960-scroll" are wrong.

proposals.before: During carefree Zhengshi years Xiahou Xuan, Li Sheng, Cao Xi, and Ding Mi reopened the corporal-punishment quarrel without closure.
proposals.after: Later, in the peaceful Zhengshi years, General Who Conquers the West Xiahou Xuan, Intendant of Henan Li Sheng, Commander of the Central Army Cao Xi, and Secretary Ding Mi again debated corporal punishment, but never reached a decision.
proposals.reason: The Chinese gives the four men's offices (征西將軍, 河南尹, 中領軍, 尚書); literal error: offices omitted.

proposals.before: When Guanqiu Jian fell, Dian’s wife Lady Xun faced execution until cousin Xun Yan’s plea reached the throne.
proposals.after: When Guanqiu Jian was executed, Lady Xun, wife of his son Dian, was liable to die; her clan elder cousin Xun Yi, related by marriage to Sima Shi, petitioned the Wei emperor to beg for her life.
proposals.reason: 顗 is Xun Yi, and 與景帝姻 explains his access; literal error: "Xun Yan" misreads 顗 and the Sima connection is omitted.

proposals.before: Lady Xun offered herself as government slave to ransom Zhi.
proposals.after: Lady Xun petitioned Colonel Director of Retainers He Zeng for mercy, asking to be enslaved to the government to redeem Zhi's life.
proposals.reason: 荀氏辭詣司隸校尉何曾 names the official petitioned; literal error: He Zeng and his office are omitted.

proposals.before: Court whispers already endorsed corporal law.
proposals.after: When I formerly served as an attendant at your side, I often heard enlightened edicts saying that corporal punishment ought to be used and would benefit government.
proposals.reason: 臣昔常侍左右，數聞明詔 is Liu Song's own testimony about imperial edicts; literal error: "Court whispers" misstates the source.

proposals.before: Pei Wei briefly supervised inspections.
proposals.after: I had been appointed Secretary only three days when the Secretary of the responsible bureau fell ill, so I was temporarily ordered to go out in his place and inspect the Orchid Terrace.
proposals.reason: 臣新拜尚書始三日…權令兼出，按行蘭台 is Pei Wei's first-person account; literal error: the circumstances are omitted.

proposals.before: Low judges mirror Zhang Shi’s refusal to bend the carriage-interdiction rule.
proposals.after: Low judges mirror Zhang Shizhi’s refusal to bend the carriage-interdiction rule.
proposals.reason: 釋之 is Zhang Shizhi; literal error: the name is truncated to "Zhang Shi".

proposals.before: Royal exceptionalism stays outside bureaucratic precedent.
proposals.after: Extraordinary judgments that reward or punish outside the law, such as the Han founder executing the Chu minister for his own reasons or enfeoffing the meritless Zhao, belong to the ruler alone and are not for officials to propose.
proposals.reason: 漢祖戮楚臣…封趙氏 cites Gaozu's precedents; literal error: the examples and the ruler-only point are omitted.

proposals.before: Jin survival court judged without statutes.
proposals.after: After the court moved south of the Yangzi, when Emperor Yuan was Chancellor and the court was newly founded, deliberations and judgments did not follow the statutes; each person put forward a different view, without any standard.
proposals.reason: 元帝為丞相時 dates the passage to Sima Rui's chancellorship; literal error: the emperor and the setting are omitted.

proposals.before: Early Han lacked wise ministers to defend classical law.
proposals.after: By then Xiao He and Cao Shen were dead, and men like Zhou Bo and Guan Ying could not set the principle right.
proposals.reason: 蕭曹 and 絳灌 name four Han ministers; literal error: the names are dropped.

proposals.before: Equal sentencing blocked mercy Zhong Chen protested.
proposals.after: As for the articles on public execution, these are not truly unpardonable crimes; even where no one was killed by hand, the code treats them alike and closes the way to reduction—this is what Zhong Yao and Chen Qun protested, and what Emperor Yuan paused over in pity.
proposals.reason: 鐘陳 is Zhong Yao and Chen Qun, and 元皇 is Emperor Yuan; literal error: "Zhong Chen" fuses two people into one name.

proposals.before: Kong Linzhi echoed Wang Lang opposing revival.
proposals.after: But Kong Linzhi disagreed, following the views of Wang Lang and Xiahou Xuan.
proposals.reason: 用王朗、夏侯玄之旨 names both precedents; literal error: Xiahou Xuan is omitted.

proposals.before: Xiankang justice swung between nitpicking and laxness.
proposals.after: In the Xiankang era Yu Bing liked to investigate and censure, to the point of pettiness; later he overcorrected and became lenient again, so strictness and laxity followed whim and the statutes were of no use.
proposals.reason: 庾冰好為糾察 names Yu Bing as the actor; literal error: Yu Bing is omitted.

proposals.before: Retired counselor Dong Zhongshu still advised Zhang Tang on classical jurisprudence, yielding 232 Spring and Autumn case rulings grounded in canonical debate.
proposals.after: When former Chancellor of Jiaodong Dong Zhongshu retired because of age and illness, the court repeatedly sent Commandant of Justice Zhang Tang to his humble lane to consult him on policy questions; Dong Zhongshu then composed the Spring and Autumn Adjudications of 232 cases, answering from the classics in detail.
proposals.reason: The existing proposed wording leaves Zhang Tang as the nearest subject of “he then composed,” but 於是作《春秋折獄》 refers to Dong Zhongshu. Naming Dong Zhongshu again removes the residual attribution error.

proposals.before: Wang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
proposals.after: Liang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
proposals.reason: 統 is Liang Tong, the memorialist introduced in s0050. The existing proposal repairs only the parallel idiomatic field.

proposals.before: The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Wang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
proposals.after: The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Liang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
proposals.reason: 統 is Liang Tong, not Wang Tong. The existing proposal repairs only the parallel idiomatic field.

proposals.before: Han verdict digests yielded three hundred further fascicles after Decree A, while Minister Bao cataloged marriage suits into the Comparative Index—960 scrolls total.
proposals.after: Han-era case decisions were collected as Ordinance A and following in more than three hundred chapters, while Minister over the Masses Lord Bao compiled decisions on marriage and litigation as the Legal Comparisons Catalogue, 906 scrolls in all.
proposals.reason: 九百六卷 is 906, not 960, and 司徒鮑公 supplies Lord Bao's office. The existing proposal repairs only the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: At Guanqiu Jian’s execution his son Dian’s wife Lady Xun faced collateral death; her clansman Yan, tied by marriage to Emperor Jing, memorialized the Wei emperor begging mercy.
proposals.after: At Guanqiu Jian’s execution, his son Dian’s wife Lady Xun faced collateral death; her elder kinsman Xun Yi, connected by marriage to Sima Shi, memorialized the Wei emperor to beg for her life.
proposals.reason: 顗 is Xun Yi, not Yan, and 景帝 here is Sima Shi. The existing proposal repairs only the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: Specialists guarding text resemble Zhang Shi holding fast to the equal verdict on breaking the imperial avenue cordon.
proposals.after: Specialists guarding the text resemble Zhang Shizhi holding fast to the impartial verdict on breaking the imperial procession cordon.
proposals.reason: 釋之 is Zhang Shizhi; “Zhang Shi” truncates his name. The existing proposal repairs only the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: As for extraordinary judgments or rewards exceeding statute—like Han founder killing Chu ministers for private motives or enfeoffing Lady Zhao without merit—only the lord monopolizes such acts; duty clerks may not emulate.
proposals.after: As for extraordinary judgments and rewards or punishments outside the law—like the Han founder executing a Chu minister for his own reasons or enfeoffing a Zhao who had no merit—these belong to the ruler alone and are not for serving officials to propose.
proposals.reason: 趙氏 does not support identifying the recipient as “Lady Zhao”; the existing proposal repairs the idiomatic omission but leaves this invented gender in the literal field.

proposals.before: At that time Xiao He and Cao Shen had died—subordinates like Zhou Bo could not straighten principle.
proposals.after: At that time Xiao He and Cao Shen had already died, and men like Zhou Bo and Guan Ying could not set the principle right.
proposals.reason: 絳灌 names both Zhou Bo, Marquis of Jiang, and Guan Ying. The current literal field omits Guan Ying; the existing proposal repairs only the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: As for marketplace execution clauses truly not unforgivable crimes hands not killers yet statutes lump equal severity blocking mitigation paths—Zhong Chen remonstrated hence Yuan emperor pitied.
proposals.after: As for the marketplace-execution articles, these are not truly unpardonable crimes; even when no one was killed by the offender’s own hand, the code assigns the same penalty and blocks reduction. Zhong Yao and Chen Qun protested this, and Emperor Yuan paused over it in pity.
proposals.reason: 鐘陳 refers to Zhong Yao and Chen Qun, not one person named “Zhong Chen.” The existing proposal repairs only the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu decided Han-Wei precedent was too muddled to govern by and ordered the chariot general, acting Secretariat chief, and Duke of Lu to recruit jurists and engrave a definitive code—that story follows.
proposals.after: Emperor Wu decided earlier statutes were too uncertain to govern by and ordered the General of Chariots and Cavalry—acting Director of the Secretariat and Duke of Lu—to recruit talented men, revise the statutes, and establish their chapters.
proposals.reason: 車騎將軍、守尚書令、魯公 are three titles of the one official being commissioned; the current coordination reads as an order to three people.

proposals.before: Corvée delays, supply bungles, and edict disputes had been jammed into mismatched chapters; Wei isolated detention crimes once accidental overlap with capital military guilt was unwound.
proposals.after: Corvée delays, supply failures, and failures to carry out edicts had been scattered across mismatched chapters; because Emperor Wen of Han’s Dingyou edict was no longer fit to serve as standing law, Wei separated these cases into the Detention Statute.
proposals.reason: 《丁酉詔書》，漢文所下 explicitly attributes the edict to Emperor Wen of Han; the current idiomatic field omits both the named ruler and the edict.

proposals.before: Under Sima Shi co-rule, daughters married out still died for parental treason.
proposals.after: When Sima Shi served as regent, Wei law still executed daughters who had married out for a parent’s great treason.
proposals.reason: 景帝輔政 says Sima Shi assisted the government as regent; “co-rule” incorrectly makes him a co-sovereign.

proposals.before: the third year of Taishi (267 CE) saw the finished code presented to the throne.
proposals.after: In the third year of Taishi, the completed code was presented to the throne.
proposals.reason: The Chinese supplies only 泰始三年. The parenthetical Western year is not asserted by the current source and should not be introduced without separately reviewed calendar evidence.

proposals.before: Punch Names threads severity of offenses, corrects scales of increase and decrease, releases manifold meanings across chapters, repairs insufficient clauses, and aligns overarching frameworks.
proposals.after: Punishment Names sets out the relative severity of offenses, corrects the gradations of increase and reduction, clarifies the many meanings of the other chapters, supplements insufficient articles, and aligns their overarching principles.
proposals.reason: 《刑名》 is Punishment Names; “Punch Names” is a definite title corruption.

proposals.before: Recaptured rebels lose hair repeatedly—sentence spawning sentence;
proposals.after: Convicts guilty of serious offenses who escape and let their hair grow past three inches are shaved again—punishment spawning punishment;
proposals.reason: 重犯亡者 are serious offenders who escape, not rebels, and 發過三寸 is a specific condition omitted by the current field.

proposals.before: castration follows rapists likewise.
proposals.after: those guilty of illicit sex are castrated on the same reasoning.
proposals.reason: 淫者 denotes offenders guilty of illicit sexual conduct; the source does not narrow the category to rape.

proposals.before: Now take lighter capital cases and thrice-escaped lewd bandits—replace all with corporal sentences.
proposals.after: Now the lighter cases within the range of capital punishment, together with those who have committed escape, illicit sex, or theft three times, should all have corporal punishment substituted for death.
proposals.reason: 三犯逃亡淫盜 describes three-time offenders in the categories of escape, illicit sex, or theft; “thrice-escaped lewd bandits” fuses those categories into one description.

proposals.before: Demote borderline capitals and chronic sex-thieves to mutilation.
proposals.after: Substitute corporal punishment for the lighter capital cases and for offenders convicted three times of escape, illicit sex, or theft.
proposals.reason: The current field collapses the separate offenses 逃亡、淫、盜 into “sex-thieves” and omits the three-offense threshold.

proposals.before: Adult repeat offenders receive no quarter.
proposals.after: Anyone outside these exempt groups who commits a crime must be punished without pardon; this is the principle of government.
proposals.reason: 自非此族 refers to everyone outside the previously named old, young, and infirm groups; neither adulthood nor repeat offending appears in the source.

proposals.before: Legal officers of fifth rank and above may lodge dissenting readings.
proposals.after: Legal officers and their superiors may submit differing opinions when their interpretations diverge.
proposals.reason: 法吏以上 does not specify the fifth rank; that rank is invented in the current field.

proposals.before: Non-capital crimes received death.
proposals.after: Thieves, illicit-sex offenders, and fugitives have killed no one and should therefore receive corporal rather than capital punishment.
proposals.reason: 則加之以刑 advocates applying corporal punishment to the listed non-homicide offenders; the current field reverses the argument by saying they received death.

proposals.before: Yuanxing era Huan Xuan reopened corporal debate.
proposals.after: At the end of Emperor An’s Yuanxing era, regent Huan Xuan again proposed restoring amputation of either foot as a substitute for death and ordered the hundred officials to debate it.
proposals.reason: The current field omits Huan Xuan’s regency, the specific proposal to amputate either foot, its purpose of reducing death sentences, and his order for an official-wide debate.

proposals.before: Zhang Pei lists gesture and expression lexicons for inferring intent.
proposals.after: Raised hands resemble begging; lowered hands resemble snatching; cupped hands resemble apology; pointing hands resemble petitioning; folded arms resemble turning oneself in; rolled-up sleeves resemble combat; solemn bearing resembles majesty; a cheerful face resembles good fortune; joy, anger, sorrow, and delight show in voice and countenance.
proposals.reason: Chinese at s0296 enumerates gesture/expression parallels without 張裴; replace summary-only idiomatic that invents Zhang Pei with a complete rendering of each parallel.

decisions.after: Raised hands resemble begging; lowered hands resemble snatching; cupped hands resemble giving thanks; mimicking-hand gestures resemble pleading; folded arms resemble turning oneself in; rolled-up sleeves resemble combat; solemn bearing resembles majesty; a cheerful face resembles good fortune; joy, anger, sorrow, and delight show in voice and countenance.
decisions.reason: Independent witness review approve_with_idiomatic_correction at efb80ded: s0296 Chinese is gesture-only (仰手似乞…貌在聲色) with no 張裴; 謝 is thanks not apology; 擬手 is mimicking-hand gestures / 訴 pleading. Primary Chinese witness for Zhang Pei remains 張裴 at s0252 on p153.
